Steam Frame - Optics
(Image credit: Future) The Steam Frame's optics are, on paper, the least exciting thing about it. We've seen a handful of headsets with similar configurations, from the Quest 3 to the Pico 4 Ultra ; neither of which are brand new.
Graphical fidelity feels much the same on the Steam Frame as the Quest 3. There's an amount of aliasing (jaggies) on straight lines and sharp details, which adds a touch of flicker as your head moves around. There is also a slight hint of chromatic aberration to the edge of some brighter details, such as the Steam Frame logo upon startup, though this is quite minor.
Text is clear to read when scaled appropriately, though can get tougher to make out when it's outside of the fairly large focal area of the pancake lenses or at a greater distance. Similarly, some details in game worlds can be lost when viewed from far away, and objects with meshes can get a little distorted or flicker—something that higher-end headsets, like the Pimax Crystal Super or Dream Air, don't suffer from. Those two headsets are available with Micro-OLED displays, which offer much more vibrancy and range of colour than the Steam Frame, but for huge price tags.
(Image credit: Future) The Steam Frame is right up there with the best of them for binocular overlap.
The Steam Frame offers, more or less, a level of quality that I've become accustomed to in relatively affordable VR headsets.
Where the Steam Frame outperformed my expectations is in binocular overlap. This is the amount of an image (given as a percentage) that is covered by both left- and right-side displays at the same time. It's not as often talked about as resolution and refresh rate, but it's hugely important for long-term comfort while wearing a VR headset. The Steam Frame has a pretty high binocular overlap, according to my own testing in the 'What is my Field of View?' application (more commonly called WimFov). This is with an IPD set to 64.
Steam Frame - 77%
Meta Quest 3 - 69%
Pimax Crystal Super 50 PPD - 77%
Pimax Crystal Super Micro-OLED - 86%
Pimax Dream Air (standard FOV) - 86%
Pimax Dream Air (wide FOV) - 77%
The Steam Frame is right up there with the best of them for binocular overlap, beaten only by the Micro-OLED optics used in both the Crystal Super and Dream Air. The Quest 3 has a lower level of binocular overlap, which can lead to discomfort or worsened 3D effects, though it does depend on your IPD and various other biological factors. I tend to struggle with headsets with a low overlap over time; they strain my eyes.
Binocular overlap, as measured in WimFov
Binocular overlap on Steam Frame (note: 'Oculus Quest2' is reporting error). WimFov Binocular overlap on Meta Quest 3. WimFov Binocular overlap on Pimax Dream Air. WimFov Valve is pretty honest when it comes to the FOV. The Steam Frame's horizontal field of view (HFOV) is noted as 'up to 110 degrees', and lo and behold, I measured it at that. That's not as common as you might think. I often find the effective HFOV to be lower than the stated FOV. For example, all three of the headsets in the table below have a listed HFOV of 110 degrees.
FOV, as measured in TestHMD Horizontal field of view (HFOV)
Vertical field of view (VFOV)
Steam Frame

Meta Quest 3

Pimax Dream Air

There are a range of factors that can have an effect on effective FOV, not the least bit my own biology. Yet one big factor is the design of the padding between one's face and the lenses. Valve seems to have nailed the padding design to maximise the effective FOV; thick enough as to not be a detriment to the long-term comfort yet ensuring a one's eyeballs are right up to the lenses. Using the glasses spacer included with the Steam Frame will knock this back a touch.
Beyond the numbers, the Steam Frame's optics plonk you right into the game world. There's no visible distortion until the very extremes of the lenses, and even then it's not that bad by comparison to some. The gap around the nose is a little noticeable during gameplay, and made worse by the glasses spacer, but you have to be kinda looking out for it to notice it too much. That can be reduced with the extended light blocker in the Ergonomic Accessories Kit for an additional $59 (89 CAD / 69 EUR / 59 GBP / 99 AUD).
Future Future Future There is a degree of glare, as I find with most headsets with pancake lenses, but to a lesser extent than the Quest 3. It's only really noticeable when there's a very high level of contrast being displayed, which isn't all that often in my experience.
For the most part, when I'm trying to throw barrels, bottles, and cans at headcrabs in Half-Life: Alyx because I've run out of ammo, I'm not thinking about the FOV, binocular overlap, or glare; I'm thinking, 'Ah, ah , ah! No, no , please, just die already! Oh, god! '
That's positive, right?
Steam Frame - Performance
(Image credit: Future) The best way to play on the Steam Frame is over the included wireless adapter. It's a USB Type-A dongle providing a 6 GHz connection beamed directly at a dedicated antenna on the Frame. Another antenna on the Frame connects directly to the local Wi-Fi. The Frame actually taps both connections for game streaming from a local PC; selecting between the two in real-time for the lowest packet loss and most robust connection.
The best way to play on the Steam Frame is over the included wireless adapter.
I'm yet to notice any connection issues over the dedicated dongle, whether in my own home or in our busy office. Nor any visible dips in quality for the game being beamed across. That's really impressive, as Valve's is using what it calls Foveated Streaming to reduce the bandwidth requirements over the wireless connection. It does so by only streaming the game in the highest detail in the area where one's eyes are looking. The rest is streamed at a lower quality level. The Frame's built-in eye tracking has to keep up with your pupils to ensure a smooth experience—and it does a superb job of it.
The Frame supports a refresh rate up to 144 Hz, though it defaults to 90/72 Hz, depending on the power mode selected. In the battery-saving Playtime mode, it will only run at 72 Hz, which is pretty passable in my opinion. At the expense of battery life and processing power, it can run anywhere from 90–144 Hz in the settings menu.
(Image credit: Future) The Qualcomm Snapdragon 8 Gen 3 (SM8650) chip does a pretty good job of rendering games locally. It does, however, require gentler programming in the graphics menu.
Take Half-Life: Alyx, for example, as Valve has created a version of the game that runs natively on the Snapdragon chip. It is of much lower quality than you'll experience by streaming the game from a local PC over the provided dongle. Valve has added foveated rendering to the game (dynamically changing the rendering level based on where one's looking) in order to improve performance. Unlike foveated streaming, foveated rendering is far more noticeable in my peripheral vision.
Though Half-Life: Alyx running at all on the Snapdragon chip is impressive, as are other games that are able to run just fine after being chopped up by the two compatibility layers, Proton and FEX. Proton deals with Windows to Linux; FEX deals with x86 to Arm. I tried out a few VR and non-VR games standalone on the Steam Frame and it often dealt surprisingly well with them. These included a few Steam Frame Standalone Verified games and one that hadn't yet been checked.
Eleven Table Tennis (verified): smooth, high fps
Marvel's Spider-Man Remastered (not verified): failed to run past splash screen
Escape Room VR (verified): smooth, decent fps
Hades (verified): smooth, high fps
Marvel's Spider-Man Remastered is Steam Deck Verified; however, that doesn't mean it will run on Frame, as it using FEX as well as Proton. Essentially, there are a few more hoops to jump through.
Hades, on the other hand, runs great via both translation layers. It's likely a boon to the Frame that the game has a Vulkan version already available. If I understand it correctly, Vulkan should let Valve skip some of the translation work and improve performance. The game reached around 100 fps, so it definitely didn't seem to suffer for any of the funny business in the background. It's best to set the Steam Frame's cap to beneath this figure, anyways, as it keeps the visuals steady and stable. Once I set the system to 144 Hz, which it couldn't reliably hit in Hades, moving my head would cause the game screen to shudder.
Eleven Table Tennis is a great reminder of when low latency and high refresh really matter in VR. I've been trying to beat the silver-level AI in that game for weeks now. I had, at times, thought it impossible, especially after trying and failing on three different VR headsets (Frame, Dream Air, Quest 3).
Installing the game on the Frame and running it locally at 120 Hz, with the ergonomic straps removed from the controllers to aid my front spin, I finally cracked it. I nailed some fast return balls that the stupid cat (the AI has a cat's face, don't ask) couldn't return. It was a silky smooth experience, even on the Frame's internal 'Turnip' Adreno GPU. I feel the local processing and high refresh really helped me here; but it drained the heck outta the battery on this thing: 50% gone in under 30 minutes.
Nevertheless, the standalone functionality feels less crucial to me. I will almost always stream games from my gaming PC via the wireless connection, due to the performance, quality, and battery life improvements I'll get onto shortly.
Steam Frame - Ergonomics
(Image credit: Future) The Steam Frame weighs in at 440 grams. On my scales, it's more like 403 grams, but that's more a criticism of my crappy scales than anything else. What's important is that it is exceedingly light; the second-lightest from my own measurements.
Steam Frame: 403 g
Quest 3: 437 g
Quest 3S: 454 g
Crystal Dream Air: 280 g
Crystal OLED: 848 g
Crystal normal: 837 g
Sony PS VR2: 499 g
Comfort in a VR headset is not all about weight, but in this case, the Steam Frame's small stature helps a helluva lot. Valve has balanced the weight of the Steam Frame across the front and back of the device, with the battery as a counterweight to the headset's 'core module', containing the optics, SoC, and most other technical bits. With the weight of the battery elsewhere, the core module weighs only 157 grams. Valve has that at 185 grams but hey ho; crappy scales.
(Image credit: Future) Ample cushioning around the face and on the rear of the battery help to alleviate most discomfort from the weight of the device during play sessions. Unlike the Quest or older, heavier headsets, the weight does not feel like it is localised to your cheekbones or around the eyes. Even after hours of play to test the battery life, I didn't notice any patches of red or indentation lines on my face.
If you wear glasses, the Steam Frame is pretty accommodating. There's a spacer included in the box that adds another 4-7 mm between your face and the lenses. It's the easiest to add into the headset that I've used to date, too. It's all magnetically attached—the padding and glasses spacer can be replaced in no time at all.
(Image credit: Future) Ergonomics accessories kit
Valve is offering an Ergonomic Accessories Kit as a separate purchase alongside the Steam Frame. It costs 59 USD/89 CAD/69 EUR/59 GBP/99 AUD and includes three premium upgrades:
Controller straps w/ compatible battery doors
Extended light blocker
Top headset strap
I reckon most Steam Frame customers would buy the Ergonomic Accessories Kit without question. I probably would, too. But I've done my duty and played extensively with it fitted to the headset and without, and I have to say, it's really not a must-have.
Future Future The headset doesn't move around much with or without the added top headset strap. It is, however, useful if you're planning to pass the headset around a large group of people, as it makes it easier to adjust from person to person in a dash. I suppose if you're playing Beat Saber or anything a little more active, you may want the added support, but again, I don't think it's all that necessary.
The extended light blocker does a pretty good job of keeping light out from your nose, and that's especially true if you wear glasses like me; however, I've played mostly without and it's not been a detriment to my time in VR.
(Image credit: Future) Then there are the most contentious upgrades of the three: the controller straps. These replace the cord straps included with the controller with straps that tighten around the entire hand, akin to the Valve Index design. Once installed, I can make better use of the finger sensing features of the Steam Frame controller (capacitive buttons combined with some sensing of the lower digits) and they're easier to slip into than the standard cord option.
Future Future On the flipside, the Frame's controllers are not as elegantly designed for this sort of strap as the Index's. I had a few members of the PC Gamer team try out the Steam Frame one by one in the office, and on numerous occasions I received the feedback that they cannot comfortably reach all the buttons. Take away the straps and that issue goes away.
In my experience, the straps are an improvement for games where grip plays a large role, such as Half-Life: Alyx. I can launch an item towards me and catch it naturally without thinking twice. Whereas without the straps, I had to sorta relearn to lift and grab, as two separate movements. But I definitely don't mind using the controllers without the straps, and for playing 2D games, the more natural position without the added straps feels best.
Steam Frame - Controllers and tracking
Future Future The tracking on the Steam Frame is excellent; perhaps even its strongest feature.
It's inside-out tracking using four monochrome cameras, combined with IR illuminators for low-light conditions. Those monochrome cameras aren't the best for passthrough or XR play—they offer a rough blue fascimile of the real-world behind the headset—but they work great for mapping the movements of the headset and controllers. That means no more Base Stations, as were required with the Valve Index; just the Frame itself keeping track of its position in VR.
What impresses me most is how consistent the boundaries of the playspace seem to be when using the Frame. It's yet to lose track of a boundary, floor height, or its own location within that space in my many weeks of testing. Whether I place it on the floor, move it around, turn it off and on again, or even move furniture around it, the playspace is locked in.
(Image credit: Future) The headset does a great job with the controllers, too. The pair provided with the Frame support 6DOF and an inertial measurement unit (IMU) to correctly orient themselves in the world with excellent accuracy.
I'm yet to experience a single moment where one or both of my virtual hands go wandering off into the distance. Neither have I experienced what I will shamelessly call a floppy hand problem, where my virtual hand feels stuck on some invisible object and flops around like a fish as I try to wiggle it free. I have had both of those happen to me in the past couple of weeks with another headset, the Dream Air, but none so far with the Frame.
The Frame's controllers are similar in shape and style to those included with the Quest 3/3S. That's no bad thing; both are comfortable and intuitive. Yet Valve has also added more buttons to its latest pads, including ABXY on the right controller, a d-pad on the left controller, and bumper buttons to both.
(Image credit: Future) These extra inputs aren't required a whole lot in VR; most devices don't make use of them. They are instead useful for playing 2D games on a virtual screen within the Frame. I've been testing this out with the original Hades: dragging the screen to a massive cinema-like size and putting my gaming chair into its deepest recline. It's pretty good, and even though I think the novelty of playing on a virtual big screen is already beginning to wear off, I can see why Valve says you can slip the Frame on and then decide which game to play. It can pretty much play whatever from your library with minimal fuss and without switching controllers.
For the record, you can pair up an external controller, keyboard, or mouse to the Frame over Bluetooth, including a Steam Controller . I haven't found much need to do so as of yet.
Steam Frame - Software
(Image credit: Future) SteamOS is going places. Once limited to the Steam Deck and whatever one dared to load the ISO onto, it has since made its way into the living room and other handhelds. With the launch of the Steam Frame, the Arch Linux-based operating system breaks into the third dimension.
The Steam Frame offers a familiar interface for any PC gamer. It's just SteamOS, or Big Picture Mode, except its hovering in front of you. It has extensive menus for adjusting various settings on the Steam Frame, a status bar with some handy functions for VR, and a slightly tweaked interface for moving and enlarging windows within your expanded field of view. Otherwise, it's just Steam.
The Steam Frame wouldn't be around were it not for SteamOS, Proton, and FEX.
All your games in your library move over to the Steam Frame upon signing in. There are new categories automatically added to the interface to separate VR titles from non-VR titles, and in some cases, games are divided by those installed on the headset and those that can be streamed from a nearby PC. Once you select a game, you can click the arrow to the right of the green play button to select between playing it locally or streaming it from your gaming PC; depending on if it is installed on one or both devices.
(Image credit: Future) Valve also offers the Steam Frame Standalone Verified program to give an idea of whether a given game is going to play nicely while running on the Frame's own hardware. Few games are built for the Frame—as far as I know, it's just Half-Life: Alyx—most are going to be either Android games running through Lepton, Valve's Android container, or use translation layers, Proton and Fex, in order to be made to run on Linux and Arm.
The Steam Frame wouldn't be around were it not for SteamOS, Proton, and FEX. Meta has Horizon OS, Google has Android XR, and Apple has visionOS for their respective headsets. Only Horizon OS feels in any way a fit for gaming, but even so, Meta has shifted to a more XR-centric interface and put a hold on third-party headsets using it . So that's out. That really means Valve had no other option than to do it itself with the Steam Frame.
And thank God for that. The biggest selling point for of the Steam Frame and SteamOS in virtual reality for me is that Meta has nothing to do with it. While you no longer need a Meta account for the Quest 3/3S, you still have to use the services of a company with big AI aspirations and a problematic privacy and safety record.
(Image credit: Future) As for games available for the Steam Frame, it has plenty to choose from already on Steam, and it's set to benefit from Valve recently adding support to Steam for Android games. The Steam Frame also comes with a free copy of Half-Life: Alyx, and I can think of no better game that this to show off what it can do; able to both be streamed from a gaming PC and run locally on the Steam Frame's Snapdragon processor. It's the best VR game around today, despite being released over six years ago.
That touches on one issue facing VR in general today: the availability of new games and experiences. Plenty of the best VR games are the same ones we have been playing for many years, such as Beat Saber, Phasmophobia, Skyrim, Blade & Sorcery, Job Simulator, Arizona Sunshine; which I've pulled from Steam's own popularity rankings, among a sprinkling of newer titles. One newer title I've really enjoyed in the past year is Ghost Town , made by Fireproof Games, but even it is a year old now.
While Steam itself sees ever-increasing numbers of games published to the platform every single year, virtual reality games published on the platform have plummeted since an initial surge around 2017-18. Meanwhile, the Meta Horizon Store appears to still be trending upwards each year , though I can't be sure how many of those are actual games. A lot seem to be training applications.
If Valve can attract new developers to share their existing and future Android games on Steam, perhaps we will see a renewed surge of VR games on the platform. As of right now, it feels like fresh experiences are few and far between.
Steam Frame - Battery
(Image credit: Future) You don't have to constantly worry about tripping over a cable with the Steam Frame. Instead, you have to be aware of your battery level.
The Steam Frame comes with a 21.6 Wh Li-ion battery, located at the rear of the strap. It has a USB 2.0 Type-C port off at an angle from its left-hand side, which is used pretty exclusively for charging the device due to bandwidth limitations for data.
There isn't an adapter included with the headset. Instead, it can be charged with any suitable power adapter up to 45 watts.
Valve is selling its own adapter for $29 (49 CAD/39 EUR/29 GBP/49 AUD). While I'm personally not too bothered about the lack of charger in the box—I have plenty already and I'm all for cutting out excess chargers—some of my colleagues feel it's a bit of a miss at this price point.
It takes a while to fully charge the Steam Frame from flat. In one test, using a 140 W Anker power adapter, it took 151 minutes to go from completely empty to fully charged. In another, using Valve's own power adapter, it took 142 minutes. So a good two hours and change for a full charge.
Here are the battery levels and times recorded from my testing:

Using a power meter on my wall outlet, I recorded the power draw in both tests around ~ 11 W at all times.
I asked Valve about the battery charging behaviour ahead of launch. They told me:
"An empty battery takes around two hours to charge to full capacity. However, the charging is not linear. There is fast charging from 0 to 65%, and regular charging from 65% and up. Charging to 65% is expected to take less than 40 minutes. (Note: these values may be optimized over time, and are therefore subject to change.)"
I hadn't seen any sign of fast charging to 65% in my own tests at the time I reached out; however, prompted by Valve's response, I tried one last test. I ran the battery down to near-flat, and while the headset was still turned on but not playing any games, I plugged in the charger.

I have felt a little impatient with the Frame on a few occassions—a feeling of having to wait too long between sessions once the battery had died. Though I did improve things by not letting the Steam Frame die completely between charges, using a suitably powerful power bank in my pocket (around 25 W should do it), and using the Frame's various power saving modes.
(Image credit: Future) Depending on the mode of use, the Steam Frame can last between one and two hours of play time:
Half-Life: Alyx (Arm version, running locally): 63 minutes
Half-Life: Alyx (streaming from PC w/ Frame set to Playtime mode): 114 minutes
So, for every hour played in a game running on the headset, you'll be more or less charging for two; however, the longevity of the headset while streaming from a PC is pretty impressive.
I took these figures with the Frame set to Playtime mode, which favours battery life over performance and limits the frame rate to 72. You can push higher performance at a cost to longevity.
I noted the power draw of the headset in each mode while playing Half-Life: Alyx. When the game is running natively on the Steam Frame in standalone mode, the whole system draws around 17-19 W. Instead beam the game from my gaming PC using the included dongle and the Frame draws as little as 10 W. Nearly half as much power draw; nearly double the battery.
(Image credit: Future) There may be another option for extending the Frame's battery life in future, too. Valve has confirmed to us it is working on a new strap with hot-swappable batteries and BMR drivers to match the excellent speakers on the Valve Index. This will be a swap-in upgrade for the modular Frame. No launch information for that one just yet, though.
As for the controllers, I'm yet to swap the AA battery located in each one since I began testing. Still going strong today at 74%.
Steam Frame - Value
(Image credit: Future) Everyone's disappointed by the RAM crisis.
Joy Lyons, Valve
There's only one Steam Frame worth buying. That's the 256 GB model. It's a VR headset that works best when streaming games installed on your gaming PC, and if you want to take advantage of the standalone functionality, there's an SD card slot for easy expansion.
That 256 GB model costs $1,059. So let's compare that price to its competition. The Steam Frame costs:
76.5% more than a Quest 3 512 GB;
8.6% less than a Bigscreen Beyond 2E, or 10% more than the Bigscreen Beyond 2;
53.9% less than a Pimax Dream Air;
6% more than a Valve Index at launch;
202% more than a Quest 3S 128 GB.
The Steam Frame is not as affordable as I'd like it to be. Nor my colleagues, some of whom literally winced as I told them the price. It's also more costly than Valve's original price target.
I wish we could have shipped it at the price that we were at last year.
Jeremy Selan, Valve
"We set out to design this hardware with one particular price in mind," says Joy Lyons, hardware engineer at Valve, "... that price target shifted just due to the ongoing RAM crisis around the world."
"We're happy to have our customers be able to have hardware during this RAM crisis, and we think it's important to launch new hardware out there and have new experiences available. But, yeah, I think everyone's disappointed by the RAM crisis."
I wish I could go one review without mentioning the damned memory crisis, or one chat with Valve without bringing it up. It has undoubtedly put a dampener on the excitement I felt for the Frame coming out of Valve's office in Bellevue nearly a year ago. One of the people that ecstatically showed off the Steam Frame to me during that visit was Jeremy Selan, a software engineer at Valve working on the Frame.
I had a chance to catch up with Selan again recently, and I asked him, 'if you could click your fingers and change anything about the Steam Frame today, what would it be?' Selan responded, "Price. I wish we could have shipped it at the price that we were at last year."
That's a question I stole from our Andy Edser during an interview he ran earlier this year with Valve on the Steam Machine. The response then from engineer Yazan Aldehayyat was much the same: "Make it cheaper".
(Image credit: Future) So if you're disappointed about the price of the Steam Frame, you're not wrong to be, nor are you alone in that sentiment. It sucks.
What's tricky for Valve is that Meta seems to have inventory or money enough to have staved off another price hike for the Quest 3. For now, at least. The company raised the price of both the Quest 3 and Quest 3S in April, though remains at lower price than Valve can offer for not totally dissimilar hardware. Meta said at the time of that price hike, "we’re making this change because the cost of building high-performance VR hardware has risen significantly." And if trillion-dollar Meta is feeling it, you can bet Valve is too.
(Image credit: Future) I wouldn't chastise someone for buying a Quest 3. You do get a lot for your money, even after the price hike. Yet if it were me with some money to burn on a VR headset today, I'd buy the Steam Frame. Convenience is king; and the Steam Frame has it nailed. While I might be in the minority of PC Gamer writers surveyed about this, I'd be willing to pay more for the ease of use and comfort provided by the Frame.
I'd also be willing to pay a bit more for the upgradeability that is being talked about here. It's only after taking the core module out myself and chatting to Valve about the modularity of the device that I've begun to realise why it's called the Steam Frame.
There's potential for plenty of upgrades here. From the full-colour RGB passthrough module from Arcturus that I've just started playing around with, or the hot-swappable battery strap from Valve, to whatever modders turn their mind to next. Building out my own Steam Frame to suit my needs over time is an exciting prospect.

title: Steam Frame starts at $1,059 and you'll want to enter the stock lottery before September 17 for a higher chance of getting one this year
text:
The Steam Frame is ready for launch, and Valve has finally announced pricing and availability for its streaming/standalone VR headset.
There are two models of the Steam Frame available:
Steam Frame (256 GB) w/ VR controllers: 1,059 USD/ 1,529 CAD/ 1,049 EUR/ 889 GBP/ 1,609 AUD/ 4,539 PLN
Steam Frame (1 TB) w/ VR controllers: 1,299 USD/ 1,859 CAD/ 1,279 EUR/ 1,089 GBP/ 1,969 AUD/ 5,549 PLN
Valve has two additional purchase available alongside the Steam Frame at launch.
There's the Ergonomic Accessories Kit. This costs 49 USD/ 69 CAD/ 59 EUR/ 49 GBP/ 89 AUD/ 229 PLN and includes two hand straps (similar to the Valve Index's), over-the-head strap, and extended light blocker.
There's also a power adapter, which costs 29 USD/49 CAD/39 EUR/29 GBP/49 AUD. There's not one included in the box, though any USB Type-C charger of 45 W should cut it if you want to save the cash.
(Image credit: Future) How to sign up for a Steam Frame at launch
If you don't mind the price, signups for a Steam Frame reservation can be made anytime between now and September 17 at 10 am Pacific Time on the product page .
Valve will be doing a one-time randomisation to determine who has a unit reserved for them and who is stuck on the waitlist. This takes place on September 17. From this, Valve will determine who has a unit reserved in their name and who is stuck on the waitlist.
Here's Valve on how the reservation system works:
Folks can sign up for the model they’d like to purchase between September 14 and September 17 at 10 am Pacific Time
When signups close, we’ll do a one-time randomization to determine reservation and waitlist order
Based on the results of that randomization, customers receive an email later on the 17 indicating they are on the reservation list or waitlist
Anyone coming to the product page after September 17 at 10 a.m. Pacific Time will be able to join the waitlist and will be added to the back
We expect to send the first batch of purchase emails out on September 18, and will continue sending those out as units become available to ship
For those on the waitlist, it means their place in line is beyond the number of Steam Frames currently available for reservation, and we will notify folks if and when they are moved into the reservation queue.
It's a similar system to the one Valve used for the launch of the Steam Machine , which so far seems to be working as intended. Orders for the Linux box were said to be going out daily back in July, with Valve believing then that it will be done with the reservation queue for the Steam Machine by the end of the year . In some regions, it had already begun offering units to those on the waitlist.
"We found the reservation system to be helpful in limiting resellers and improving the purchase experience," says Valve.
The Steam Frame is a different beast altogether, with a varied range of components and heaps of LPDDR5X memory chips, which could make life more difficult for Valve, but it seems the reservation system is at least working as intended. The main thing to note is that, by signing up ahead of September 17, you secure the best chance at a Steam Frame anytime soon.

title: Valve working on Steam Frame strap that adds Index-like speakers and hot-swappable batteries, 'coming soon'
text:
The Valve Index might be outdated in many ways today, but it still holds a special place in my heart for its excellent audio solution: twin speakers that deliver impressive spatial properties without actually touching your ears. The Steam Frame doesn't take the same approach, sadly, but word from Valve is that it's working on a first-party accessory that'll add a set of Index-like speakers to the compact Frame.
The Steam Frame is modular. Three small switches are all it takes to completely remove the core module, containing the chip, RAM, storage, optics and more, from the strap. The strap also includes the battery, SD card slot, and speakers.
"So the battery, the thermals; I think those will be the ultimate limits of the device," said Jeremy Selan, software engineer at Valve during a pre-launch chat. "We thought of that early. It's no surprise. So that's why we were very proud of making a modular design where the core module is separate from the rear.
"And in fact, you might say, 'Hey, what is Valve going to do with this?' We're working on a future first-party accessory where it will plug in and replace the existing [strap]. That head strap will include a hot-swappable battery, and then premium Index-style off-ear audio."
When pushed for a date as to when this accessory might be available, Selan joked that he was one of the people who was confident that the Steam Frame would land in early '26, and no longer felt like a credible source on these things. Fair enough. He ended up saying, "we're working to make it available as soon as we can."
"The Valve Index audio is, I mean, it's awesome, and so we wanted to give people the opportunity to have that," says Joy Lyons, hardware engineer and audio expert at Valve. "And so it's a modular design. You just snap in, like Jeremy mentioned. That's not available at launch, but it's coming soon, and we'll have pricing and details on that."
The Valve Index with its excellent off-ear speakers. (Image credit: Future) The Steam Frame's speaker system is totally serviceable, anyways. I've been using the headset for three weeks and I've no complaints in that specific department. Lyons explained how this solution ended up being implemented.
"One of the design principles for the headset is being lightweight and also being portable, so you can collapse it. And so having any additional structure in the headband, that was something where early on it was clear, hey, that's going to interfere with our ability to collapse it and take it with you. And so we elected to put the audio into the head strap."
(Image credit: Future) Lyons explained how they decided on two drivers on either side of the headset, but that these ended up pretty close to the core module. The core module contains all the camera and sensors for the Frame's inside-out tracking, which makes it very sensitive to vibration.
"The vibration caused the screen to jump with the bass, which is not as exciting as it sounds," Lyons said.
"So we were able to, with that early architecture, flip one of the drivers, and so the sound's coming out in phase. So you're getting your double sound output per side, but the vibration's been cancelled. And so we wanted to have this open-ear experience, so that really gives you that sense of immersion; you're not closed in, you're not hot, and it just builds a very natural sound."

title: Valve targeted a lower price for the Steam Frame, then the memory crisis happened: 'I wish we could have shipped it at the price that we were at last year'
text:
After many years of waiting and a few false starts over on Reddit , the Steam Frame is finally here. We even have a price for the virtual reality headset, which is set to ship imminently to customers. Hold onto your headsets…
Steam Frame (256 GB) w/ VR controllers: 1,059 USD/ 1,529 CAD/ 1,049 EUR/ 889 GBP/ 1,609 AUD/ 4,539 PLN
Steam Frame (1 TB) w/ VR controllers: 1,299 USD/ 1,859 CAD/ 1,279 EUR/ 1,089 GBP/ 1,969 AUD/ 5,549 PLN
An additional Ergonomic Accessories Kit is available to purchase alongside the Frame. It includes two hand straps for the controllers, a head strap for the headset, and an extended light blocker. This costs 49 USD/ 69 CAD/ 59 EUR/ 49 GBP/ 89 AUD/ 229 PLN.
Be honest, were you expecting this sorta price for the Steam Frame? Some called it, due to the similar cost of a Valve Index for most of its lifespan; though I expect many of us adjusted our expectations following the onset of the memory crisis, and the subsequent launch of the Steam Machine . Our Andy called that the biggest victim of the RAMpocalypse , and you could argue something similar for the Steam Frame.
It's certainly been a journey for Valve. A week prior to the Steam Frame's launch, we spoke with two engineers at Valve about the project: Joy Lyons, hardware engineer, and Jeremy Selan, software engineer. The memory crisis and the price were a big part of that conversation. From that chat, we can confirm that Valve had aimed for a lower price point than the one it's launching the Frame for today.
Here's Lyons on the memory crisis:
"We set out to design this hardware with one particular price in mind, but we've made choices to make sure that we're making a product that is choiceful, that people can purchase, they can upgrade with different features later. But we wanted to make sure we had a base product with really great performance. Then that price target shifted due to the ongoing RAM crisis around the world."
Lyons also said that forecasting for the cost of certain components used in the Steam Frame is an ongoing challenge.
"We don't know what pricing is in the future. We try to monitor these things, but we're certainly very aware of it.
"We think it's a great, compelling product, and we are still happy to have it out there. We're happy to have our customers be able to have hardware during this RAM crisis, and we think it's important to launch new hardware out there and have new experiences available. But, yeah, I think everyone's disappointed by the RAM crisis."
(Image credit: Future) Selan was the person that guided me through the Steam Frame and all of its features back at Valve's HQ in late 2025. They also lament the increase in price since that time: "I wish we could have shipped it at the price that we were at last year. It's still awesome today. It is amazing, but we were targeting a lower price, and I wish we could have done that."
The price puts the Steam Frame at a big disadvantage to the Quest 3 . Even following a price hike, which Meta justified on similar terms to Valve , you can buy a Quest 3 for $600 today. Admittedly, I feel the Steam Frame is a better all-round device than the Quest 3, but the significantly higher price point of the Frame does leave the Quest 3 fairly unchallenged in the mainstream market, especially when it offers a similar level of fidelity to the Frame.
Memory is one factor for the Steam Frame's higher cost; the Frame has 16 GB of LPDDR5X RAM, while the Quest 3 has 8 GB of LPDDR5. We asked Lyons and Selan about this decision and whether there was any discussion of shipping the Frame with less memory to save on cost.
The Ergonomics Accessories Kit for the Steam Frame costs $49 extra, but you don't need it. (Image credit: Future) "We looked at the Steam Frame pre-launch a few years ago, we said we can access this huge fraction of the same catalog [as the Steam Deck], or we can slice a major component off it and make sure that'll never run, if we do a lower limit," said Selan. "Now, granted, the trade-offs and cost and performance were a little different at that time, but even in hindsight, having a single target where we know what this generation will be capable of running is great, and we're very happy with that."
Meta also has the benefit of happily burning billions every quarter on its Reality Labs division , which is responsible for its Meta Quest headsets as well as its latest Orion smart glasses. While Valve isn't exactly strapped for cash, as far as cash flow goes, very few companies can spend as much as Meta without seeing much return on investment and not worry about it. That doesn't change much from a customer perspective, mind, many of whom will now have to weigh up whether Valve's device is worth an extra $450. Tough call.

title: Forget GTA 6, I have brought GTA 5 closer to being the true greatest game of all time: Hulk – Ultimate Destruction
text:
Los Santos Customs
I'm modding GTA 5 every day in a quest to either transform it into a PC version of GTA 6 or break it entirely. Come back tomorrow to find out what new horrible thing I've done to Rockstar's baby, or check out what I got up to earlier .
Here's some logic for you: Grand Theft Auto 6—fattened on its billions—cannot help but be the greatest game of all time. This I have gathered from the apocalyptic euphoria that surrounds its release. But GTA 6 is not out yet, and the greatest game of all time, currently, is The Incredible Hulk: Ultimate Destruction for the PlayStation 2, original Xbox, and GameCube.
Ergo, QED, post hoc ergo propter hoc, abracadabra: GTA 6 will basically be like The Incredible Hulk: Ultimate Destruction.
With that key fact in mind, and with the aim of continuing to transform Grand Theft Auto the fifth into a facsimile of GTA 6 (this time on PC), I have installed Superman V into GTA 5. Your heroes now have laser eyes (also cryo eyes, pulse eyes, solar flare eyes, and so on), super speed, freeze breath, the ability to fly, and X-ray vision—which so far as I can tell is a heat-haze effect that happens intermittently.
I have waved goodbye to guns, much like the protagonist of A Farewell To Arms, who also probably did that after learning he could set people on fire by staring at them.
It works alarmingly well. I can ignite passing cars with my heat vision, freeze cops where they stand, and subject Los Santos' now-roving ambient hit squads to the carcinogenic effects of sustained X-ray exposure. I can also fly, which sometimes works, and sometimes results in Franklin, Michael, or Trevor tumbling lazily but uncontrollably through the sky, like an airborne flower.
Also, I can do this now. (Image credit: Rockstar) My only concern is that, at this point, I am rapidly running out of keys on my keyboard with which to activate the various mods I have installed. At time of writing, hitting any of my function keys will summon a pile-up of distinct mod menus: Enhanced Native Trainer, Menyoo, the one that controls giving people piggybacks , the one that controls summoning dogs . What if what breaks by the end of this thing is not GTA 5, but my ability to control it?

title: Lies of P publisher files trademark for likely sequel 'Wonders of O'
text:
First reported by Phrasemaker , Lies of P publisher Neowiz has filed an EU trademark for something called "Wonders of O" categorized as, among other, similar things, a bit of "virtual reality game software." While not 100% confirmed, there's a strong possibility that this is the Lies of P sequel we know is in development.
Similarly, it's difficult to see it being anything other than a Wizard of Oz adaptation in the same way Lies of P was a sicko's souslike Pinocchio. The name aside, Lies of P's post-credits scene ended with a view of a woman in ruby slippers clicking her heels⁠—prepare yourself for the tragic Cowardly Lion boss fight now, it'll be easier that way.
It just feels right, don't it? They're both fairy tales published in the Victorian era⁠—1881 for P, 1900 for O⁠—and while defined in the popular imagination by later Hollywood golden age film adaptations, the original works are far weirder and more interesting than most people give them credit for.
It seems like the marketing machine is starting to heat up for The Wonders of O. A few weeks ago, Lies of P developer Nough, formerly Round 8, put out a mini documentary hyping up its name change and work on the Lies of P sequel. Back in 2023, PCG news writer Lincoln Carpenter liked Lies of P well enough in his 74% review , but at the end of last year, our colleague Harvey Randall expressed his excitement for the studio's next game based on the quality of Lies of P's Overture expansion .

title: Valve had next-gen VR 'headsets ready three, four years ago and they were big, bulky devices' but went back to the drawing board after actually putting them on
text:
The Steam Frame is here and it's one of the best VR headsets I've ever had attached to my face, just don't ask me about the price. But when we spoke to two of the people at Valve who helped create the device—Joy Lyons and Jeremy Selan—they told me the company actually had its new VR headsets ready years ago, but they made the tough decision to pull the plug on those designs.
"We had the headsets ready three, four years ago," Selan explains, "and they were big, bulky devices. They were more in the style of the Valve Index , and we put them on, and we're just like, this doesn't feel like what we would want the next round of our product to be."
We'd asked why now, why is this the right time to release a new VR headset? With sales dropping year over year and 2026 potentially being the worst year effectively since records began for PCVR releases, it doesn't necessarily seem like the perfect time to be putting out new virtual reality hardware, and that's before we even mention the memory and hardware pricing crisis.
"You asked, why now?" says Selan. "The answer with all Valve projects is 'as soon as we can'. Right, this was the soonest we could release the headset, but we had to make sure it was ready.
"The hardware engineers went back to the drawing board many, many times to finally achieve sort of the very small form factor, the comfortable, the lightweight. Figuring out all the system trade-offs with regards to power versus battery weight, versus cooling, and thermals. So this was absolutely the fastest we were capable of shipping the device that we were proud of.
"Now we thought that was going to be early 2026, and it turns out due to supply and component shortages and economics that in fact now was the soonest we could release it."
But it's not just about the hardware. As Valve engineer Joy Lyons notes, "The focus was on being lightweight and being comfortable", but while it's the hardware that makes that possible, all of the work Valve has been putting in with its previous releases on the software side have made this headset the one that actually gets released.
"We learned a lot with our portable systems," Lyons explains, "including the Steam Deck launch and all the work we did for emulation and the operating system, with Proton being able to run Windows-based games on Linux, on the SteamOS operating system.
"And so we've been continuing that work, and now we've got an ARM device, and so we think this is a great time to take advantage of Proton, being able to do FEX, which allows us to run x86 games on a piece of ARM hardware, and Lepton, which is the new work to do Android-based games, and have that work also on our SteamOS platform. And so we're able to have all these come together, as well as all of our work on the hardware side."
Future Future Future It's this kind of VR nexus point which has made the Steam Frame the right device for Valve, and at the right time. It is, of course, a PC VR device, with its almost uncanny ability to stream games wirelessly from your PC utterly seamlessly, but it is also a standalone device able to translate your x86 PC's Steam library and have that run inside an ARM-based VR headset. Again, almost seamlessly.
And then you also now have the ability to play Android games through Steam via the Lepton translation layer. Now, that's not just Candy Crush writ large on a massive virtual screen, this is specifically designed to capture the wealth of VR content released for the Meta Quest and its Android-based Horizon OS. And with this new world of potential content available to the Steam Frame as a portable device, it's been a bit of a journey of discovery even for Valve.
"I'm like, 'I wonder if this one will run?'" says Lyons. "And you download it, and you open it, and it runs, and you put it on the huge screen. That was the moment where it's just like, 'this is fun. I'm gonna take off my engineer hat. I'm gonna stop nitpicking every little thing that I know about the device, and I'll definitely address that tomorrow. But right now, I'm actually having fun.'
"I think I went through 89 games in a two week period… that's kind of the moment where it's like, 'yeah, this is great'."
"We're our own best testers," adds Selan. "So I do remember in those days I would have access to this secret prototype VR hardware, and I would take it home… and I'd still use my Steam Deck.
"And there became a transition point with this round of hardware, where when I took this home and this was my favorite device to use. And so, for me personally, that's when sort of a switch flipped in my head, and I was like, 'This is going to be a real thing'."

title: Bungie delays next Marathon update and ends 'strict seasonal schedule' as it goes all-in on Destiny-like features
text:
Bungie is changing how it updates Marathon going forward, saying it is "moving away from a strict seasonal schedule to give the team more flexibility to build, test, and improve features before release." As a result, the content planned to launch as part of this month's seasonal refresh has been delayed into December , and will be preceded by a small update in October "that resets progression and the in-game economy, refreshes rewards, and improves the live game."
The Nightfall refresh, launching on October 6, will give all Marathon players "a fresh starting point," something Bungie said was necessary after issues with the season "accelerated some players into the endgame while leaving others behind."
We’re making changes to Marathon’s update plans and how we deliver new content.We’re moving away from a strict seasonal schedule to give the team more flexibility to build, test, and improve features before release. (1/2)
— @marathonteam.bungie.net ( @marathonteam.bungie.net.bsky.social ) 2026-09-14T18:19:57.929Z "This made Extraction more difficult to engage with and prevented the reset from working as intended," Bungie wrote. "October gives us an opportunity to apply what we learned and establish a healthier progression experience."
The October refresh will also see the Vault Breaker PvE mode brought back for a limited time, and there will be other "gameplay experiments" between the October refresh and Symbiosis update in December as well. That's the big one: PvE will finally be made a permanent mode, and there will be a new Runner shell, a "social space with a firing range," an experimental Team Deathmatch mode, and various other improvements.
"[Symbiosis] is only the beginning of what we’re working toward. As players spend time with these updates and share their feedback, we’ll continue refining and expanding Marathon," Bungie wrote.
"We’ll share more about that future through Dev Insights videos and regular development updates. Our first blog about Marathon’s future plans is scheduled for later this month where we will share how we will be evolving Marathon into a more alien and dynamic survival experience."
That sounds promising—I've said before and I'll probably say again that Marathon looks like a game that could really pull me in with a singleplayer mode that allows me to explore and play at my own pace—but some players aren't too happy about the considerably longer-than-expected wait for new content.
Memories of Destiny 2, which scrapped its own seasonal model in favor of "episodes" a few years ago—a move which did not save it —likely also loom large, particularly given that Marathon's concurrent player numbers on Steam continue to sag : A shakeup like this, especially for a game so relatively new, has a certain 'last ditch effort' vibe to it.
Still, there is some excitement about the prospect of a more well-rounded Marathon emerging from all of all, with a properly fleshed-out singleplayer mode and more social interactivity—which could, ironically, make Marathon much more Destiny-like. Bungie comms boss Dylan Gafner, aka dmg04, said on X that players can "expect more comms from the team over the next few weeks (and months)." We'll see how it goes.

title: The Steam Frame launches during one of the slowest periods for VR on Steam, but Valve hopes to 'rekindle the excitement' for PCVR
text:
There was a time when VR was pretty much exclusive to the PC. I'm talking about when the HTC Vive and Oculus Rift were the pinnacle of technology, circa 2016. I have very fond memories of those two headsets, often borrowing them from friends and colleagues, then ferrying them around to various spots to evangelise the new and exciting world of VR; VR that was then entirely tethered to a gaming PC. Then came the Oculus Go, later the Oculus Quest, and all of a sudden, VR was mobile.
There's a lot of unique VR content that can only be accessed with the capabilities and power of the PC and the experimentation that comes on it.
Jeremy Selan, Valve
It took a while before standalone VR headsets really took off. It wasn't until the Quest 2, and later Quest 3 / Quest 3S , that these headsets started to dominate the conversation around virtual reality. Nowadays, these three dominate the Steam Hardware Survey for August 2026 , accounting for over 60% of headsets plugged into a PC by those surveyed. The Valve Index, which launched in 2019, remains in fourth place. Few new arrivals in PCVR get anywhere close: the Bigscreen Beyond has just 1.25% of the share, which is less than the original Vive.
Many are using standalone headsets to play VR games powered by their gaming PC, hence being registered on Valve's survey at all. So, in a sense, there's still so much to play for on PC.
"Some of the other mobile devices, like the Meta Quest, for example, are some of the most popular headsets on Steam," says Jeremy Selan, a software engineer at Valve who worked on the Steam Frame. "So there is a real draw with PCVR even today amongst the millions and millions of VR headsets out there, and that's, I believe, because there's a lot of unique VR content that can only be accessed with the capabilities and power of the PC and the experimentation that comes on it."
Yet it'd be fair to say that the market has shifted attention away from PCVR experiences. I've had a look around SteamDB at the number of VR games that are released on Steam every year, and it's not a positive trend.
The number of VR games on the platform reached peak around 2017, and since that time, it's either remained flat or dropped with each subsequent year. By SteamDB's figures, 2025 was the worst year for VR games on Steam for a decade. Just 481 VR games released on the platform, and you have to go back to 2015, prior to the launch of the HTC Vive and Oculus Rift, to see a lower figure. Compare that to the exponential increase of non-VR games released on Steam each year, and it looks like VR has struggled to maintain a foothold on the platform.
(Image credit: Future) In 2017, VR games accounted for 15% of all game releases on Steam. In 2025, they accounted for just 2%.
In comparison, the Quest Store has only seen an increase in new releases each year since 2020 . Though Quest Store DB doesn't note how many of those are actual games. From a quick glance, many appear to be learning or XR experiences.
The HTC Vive Cosmos Elite with base stations and the old style of VR controller. (Image credit: Future) I'm not turning my nose up at the games that have launched on Steam in the past year, especially as that's 481 more things to play with a VR headset on PC. Moreover, many of the best VR games on PC came out years ago, such as Half-Life: Alyx, and they're still as enjoyable as ever. We're not short of things to play, but we might end up that way if something doesn't change.
The ongoing tally for 2026 suggests there have been 270 new VR games on Steam so far. We're already three quarters of the way through the year, and at this rate, we're looking at yet another poor yield; potentially the lowest since PCVR began.
(Image credit: Future) So, what might help reverse this trend? Valve hopes that its new hardware, the Steam Frame, might turn the tide for Steam's VR catalogue; or, at the very least, bridge the divide between PCVR and mobile VR for gamers and developers.
"We love the PCVR community," says Steam Frame hardware engineer Joy Lyons. "We've been making VR devices for decades now, and so we've been there since the beginning."
We see this as a sort of a broadening and maturing of the market; sort of an opening of the tent to more potential customers, more potential gamers.
Joy Lyons, Valve
The Frame offers something new for Valve. The ability to stream games from a local gaming PC over a dedicated wireless connection and run games on its very own hardware, a Snapdragon 8 Gen 3 chip. This dual functionality is nothing new for virtual reality, but from my time testing the Steam Frame over the past few weeks, it's definitely at its best when playing PCVR games streamed wirelessly via the included adapter. In that sense, it feels more a PCVR headset with standalone functionality than the other way around.
Lyons explains the rationale behind Valve's approach with the Steam Frame:
"We think it's great for customers to have more access to different types of games," Lyons says. "And I think what we're seeing is a maturing of the platform with these sort of fundamental technology movements just to make the emulation layers work, for example. And we see this as a sort of a broadening and maturing of the market; sort of an opening of the tent to more potential customers, more potential gamers."
(Image credit: Future) The Steam Frame uses Proton, FEX, and Lepton to support a wider array of games. We're pretty familiar with Proton from the Steam Deck and Steam Machine, offering a way to play games made for Windows on a Linux machine. FEX is the emulation layer that makes it possible to play games designed for x86 chips on Arm chips. Games that run well on the Steam Frame from both Proton and FEX will get a badge to say so via the Steam Frame Standalone Verified programme.
Lepton is a container for Android games using the APK file format, which will allow these to run on the Arm-powered, SteamOS-run Steam Frame. Android games are now arriving on Steam, too. This will, in turn, boost the number of newly-released VR games on Steam. It just may take some time for many of the Android games mostly made for Quest to arrive. A good way to bump the numbers for next year and beyond.
"We wanted to, with the emulation, be able to have access to more games in the VR space," Lyons says. "And so I think some people who have done PCVR maybe haven't had access to some of the APK type games and so we're growing the catalog on that side as well."
Now, you might argue that's not really expanding PCVR so much as injecting Steam with lots of mobile VR games. I guess you'd be right, you ol' stick in the mud, you. But Valve engineer Jeremy Selan also counts PCVR experiences among those that they hope to get a much-needed boost from the launch of the Steam Frame.
(Image credit: Future) "This is designed for PCVR streaming and to do that really, really well," Selan says of the Steam Frame. "So we've been giving these units out to developers. Our hope is that this will help rekindle the excitement of what you can do with PCVR.
We love the PCVR community.
Joy Lyons, Valve
"Our hope is that out of the box, obviously, no work is needed," Selan continues. "Your existing catalog of VR titles on Steam will just work. But over time, as we sell more of these and the economics improve, we think this will give a new life to the ability to take advantage of the large compute of your PC while still having a great wireless VR experience."
"We love the PCVR community," Lyons says. "We always will. This is our heritage. These are our customers, and we see this as a great product for them. We made it for them. But we also want to grow a healthy ecosystem for both the gamers and the game developers."
(Image credit: Future) I guess we'll have to check back in on the stats once the Frame has had a chance to shake things up. As Selan says in our chat, there are also some VR games that will always be tied to PC, like flight sims or racing sims, but those often feel pretty clunky in my experience. I can't even boot the latest F1 game in VR, let alone join a race. Nevertheless, I agree with Selan that more can be done with VR with a PC powering the experience.
Perhaps Valve should lead the way with its own first-party VR game, like it did Half-Life: Alyx. Of course, I asked Lyons and Selan about any plans for future release, but they told me Valve has "elected to pour all our efforts into making our partner games available," and "don't have any new titles coming out." Though, Half-Life: Alyx came out nearly a year after the Valve Index, so I'm holding out hope yet. Credulous? I don't know the meaning of the word.

title: Wardogs players are actively avoiding one team in particular: 'They are literally the dumbest people on the planet'
text:
Last night, a buddy and I were stuck on the team selection screen in Wardogs. Manticore (Green) and Valkyra (Red) were 100% full, but Lonestar (Blue) had plenty of vacancies. Yet, there we sat—locked in a stalemate with a dozen other players desperate to not join blue.
"Anything but blue," we chanted, spamming left-click over Green and Red.
It is, for some reason, understood in Wardogs that Blue team kinda sucks. It seems like a silly claim to make in an FPS where teams are scrambled every match and everyone starts with the same exact resources, but Blue's infamy began during Wardogs' closed betas and has only cemented since launch. If you're a Wardogs player, you immediately knew who this article was about.
"The battle before the battle," reads one top-upvoted post on the Wardogs subreddit, depicting a team select screen with a sparse Blue roster. Another post renames each faction according to difficulty: "Easy" for Green, "Normal" for Red, and "NIGHTMARE MODE" for Blue.
Even the devs are acknowledging Lonestar's bad rap.
"Lonestar actually did it," Bulkhead co-founder Howard Phillpott posted on X today in response to a Lonestar win screen.
To a degree, the Blue team hate is a joke that the community and devs are having fun with. Most aren't taking it super seriously, but some definitely are.
(Image credit: Team17) "They literally are the dumbest people on the planet," wrote one aggrieved Redditor , citing counterproductive behavior on his Lonestar teams, like "using the respawn vehicle to just drive circles in the FOB, not realizing no one can spawn because they keep moving it."
Last night was the first time I actively avoided Blue, which delayed me getting to play by a few minutes. In more extreme cases, an entire match can be delayed by folks dragging their feet with Lonestar.
"The server would boot up, the first 40 or so players would sort into teams, and then the match start would come to a complete halt as people refused to pick Blue," recounted Reddit user PogoMarimo . "These would be 80+ pop servers and they would go 10 minutes without launching because not enough people were willing to pick Blue to get the match to the starting population needed."
"I, of course, was one of those refusing to choose blue, because I had already done Blue duty twice that day and saw awful things happen. I'm not ashamed to admit it."
What's your favourite difficulty?  from  r/WarDogs Anecdotally, I have witnessed some truth to the Lonestar hate. Of the three matches I played last night, the two I played on Blue team were undeniable stomps—the sort of matches where Red and Green have sturdy FOBs and drill towers controlling the hot zone, while it took 45 minutes for our Blue base to construct a complete wall.
My last match of the night was on Red, and the difference was dramatic: Within 15 minutes, a squad of dedicated building specialists had constructed a super FOB with reinforced walls, barbed wire moats, enclosed sniper towers, mortar emplacements, and a maze of doors and alleys meant to deter infiltrators. Green had a similar setup on the other side of the map, while Blue was just sort of… there.
I love everything about this clip.Never change Blues 💙(Thanks to u/pancakerulez for sharing) pic.twitter.com/BvWsRtOd6q September 14, 2026
So if there is something about Blue, what is it, exactly?
One popular theory is that Lonestar is the worst team because it has fundamental disadvantages. The blue pants and patches that all members wear allegedly make them easier targets in forested areas. I think there's some truth to this, especially the blue jeans of it all, but none of the factions camouflage particularly well out in the open (an intentional bit of design, I reckon). But perhaps Lonestar has it worse than the others.
(Image credit: Bulkhead) The other theory is that Lonestar beginning in the southernmost corner of the map, while Manticore and Valkyra begin in the West and East, sets the Blue faction up for a two-front war. I think this could have some merit—it is notable that the headquarters aren't lined up a perfect 120 degrees around the circumference of the zone, but it's hard to say for sure if this actually translates to a Blue team sandwich with any consistency. This talking point is coming up enough that I expect Bulkhead will chime in someday soon with data that supports or disproves it.
Another, less talked about possibility, is that Blue team's infamy is a self-fulfilling prophecy. Folks have one bad night with Lonestar and decide to believe the reputation, or hear it's the team to avoid, or notice everyone else actively avoiding it, and you end up with a Blue team full of less experienced players. It's a fascinating problem—if it even qualifies as one yet—unique to Wardogs' three-team format. Maybe I should try to buck the trend and go Blue. At least I know there's always a free seat.

title: After nearly a year of silence following its last-minute delay, Kingmakers resurfaces with an extended gameplay video and new playtest
text:
It's been just about a year since Kingmakers , the game about bringing a gun to a knife fight, was delayed just ahead of its planned launch , and we've heard nothing about it since. Today developer Redemption Road finally broke that extended silence with a new "deep dive" trailer detailing everything players will be doing in the game, and also opened the door to signups for an upcoming playtest.
First things first: I would be remiss if I didn't at least acknowledge the awkward cinematic interludes. They're really not great, and all I can say is that hopefully they're just bits of exposition built specifically for the trailer and not actually part of the game.
That aside, there's a lot going on here. Fighting large numbers of hopelessly outclassed enemies is still the central hook in Kingmakers, but you're also going to be leading armies on a strategic scale, building and managing settlements, and collecting resources so you can buy better equipment.
I'm really not sure how I feel about all that. Rolling into Bannockburn behind the wheel of a Leopard 2 has obvious appeal, but do I really want to be worrying about placing farms and erecting fortifications when I could be punching 120mm HEAT-sized holes in some peasant's hovel? But on the other side of that coin, what happens when the novelty of 'you have a sword, I have a SAW' wears off? Sooner or later it might be nice to have other things to do, especially if you're the kind of gamer who occasionally asks questions like, 'Why am I in Bannockburn with a Leopard 2?'
(The famous Battle of Bannockburn, for the record, does not actually feature in Kingmakers, which is about assisting Welsh nobleman Owain Glyndŵ in his 1403 uprising against the English.)
If you have similar questions about how the full Kingmakers experience will compare to the initial bonkersness of its 2024 reveal , the Kingmakers playtest may be a way to find answers, or at least get an early feel for which way it's headed. Go to the Steam page , mash the playtest signup button, and when (or if, I suppose) the time comes you'll receive an email notifying you that you're in.
One thing that isn't included in today's video, sorry to say, is a new release date—Kingmakers is still listed on Steam as "coming soon."

title: Arc Raiders Expeditions may not come back: 'Maybe we'll scrap the whole system'
text:
Embark Studios announced a "pause" on Expeditions in Arc Raiders until early 2027 so it can rework the system to address longstanding issues and complaints that can't be handled with "incremental fixes." In a recent interview with PCGamesN , though, Arc Raiders executive producer Aleksander Grøndal said the studio might go even further by ditching Expeditions entirely.
Expeditions are essentially Arc's equivalent of prestiging in Call of Duty: High-level players invest time and resources into a "caravan" that ultimately—within the context of the game's fiction—enables their character to leave the Rust Belt forever. Practically speaking, it's a full reset of levels, skills, and inventory, in exchange for certain unique benefits conferred upon the player's new character. It's a major undertaking, and many Arc players haven't been happy with the amount of grind involved for a relatively minor payoff.
Announcing the pause in August, Embark said many of the issues raised by players, "like the tight departure windows, the reward structure, and accessibility for new players, need more than incremental fixes. They call for bigger changes." The fifth Expedition, set to depart at the end of September, will be the last until Embark has the overhaul finished—or just cans the whole thing, as the case may be.
"Was the system perfect? No, probably not," Grøndal told PCGN at Gamescom. "We want to make some significant changes to the Expedition system. But I think right now we're focused on, 'Yeah, they are what they are,' but the intent is to have them change.
"Maybe we'll scrap the whole system altogether. That is on the table, too. Right now, the team is trying to figure out what the next steps for Expeditions are."
When Embark will make its final decision on the fate of Expeditions remains, well, undecided , although nothing's going to happen until the Frozen Trails major update drops in October. But whatever happens, it seems clear that players should expect major changes.

title: The Steam Deck 2 has 'not really' been impacted by the memory supply crisis, with Valve still focused on a 'very delineated performance improvement' for its next handheld
text:
With the release of the new Steam Controller , the Steam Machine , and now the Steam Frame VR headset, this year has been chock-full of Valve hardware releases. So, what could possibly be next—the Steam Deck 2? To some extent, sure; Valve has been " hard at work " on its next handheld gaming PC pretty much since the original Steam Deck launched back in 2022 . What's surprising, though, is that Valve claims the RAMpocalypse hasn't hugely affected its plans.
Despite the clear impact on the pricing of both the Steam Machine and the Steam Frame , Valve engineer Pierre-Loup Griffais told IGN that the memory supply crisis has "not really" affected the company's plans for the Steam Deck successor. He added, "We've talked before about how we want to make sure there's a very delineated performance improvement for something like a future Steam Deck, and I think we're still looking at it in the same way."
"It's just a matter of looking at the current conditions and seeing how and when we can deliver something like that," Griffais says, "But from what we're working on, as far as the user experience goes and what the product that we're trying to build goes, it's very similar goals."
Valve has been saying as far back as 2023 that it was waiting for " a generational leap in performance " to justify a follow-up, so that part of the strategy has remained consistent. That the company isn't rushing to push out an overpriced Steam Deck successor is arguably no bad thing either, especially given that the price for the 1 TB version of the original Steam Deck has now ballooned to $949 .
It's good to hear that the Deck 2 is still being worked on despite the ongoing memory shortage. The Steam Frame and Steam Machine were already announced and shown off essentially as finished products late last year, so those would be hard (but not impossible) to back out of. Although Valve has said it's working on a Steam Deck 2, it doesn't seem to be quite so close to release, and concerns that the company could bin the project are a bit more pertinent than with the other products.
(Image credit: Valve) Valve obviously won't attempt to squeeze the launch of the Steam Deck 2 into an already packed year, but the memory supply crisis has likely pushed the handheld's release further out too.
But just how far out could a Steam Deck 2 release be? Well, Valve itself does not see an imminent end to the supply crisis , though some major memory players predict things could improve around late 2027 or early 2028 thanks to a surge in Chinese capacity . Other predictions suggest we should only be so lucky, with both SK hynix's CEO and Phison's CEO saying demand could continue to outstrip supply until 2030.
In light of those circumstances, 'not really' feels a bit like an exercise in measured understatement to me. At any rate, here's hoping we're not waiting until 2030 for a Steam Deck successor.

title: Admitting the OGL fiasco was a 'rug pull', D&D head says 'bluntly, we're recovering from a lot of missteps—very loud, very public missteps'
text:
Dungeons & Dragons has had a rough handful of years. A new version of the Open Game Licence (OGL) leaked in 2023 , portending doom for independent creators and giving Wizards of the Coast a licence to rug-pull any third-party creator it didn't like (among other such horrors). This began the long and arduous process of mending burned bridges and un-pissing everybody off, starting with an immediate walk-back .
Since then, there have been upsets, ones I've been plenty critical of myself . But in late 2025, D&D got a new head in Dan Ayoub, who is now in charge of the D&D franchise at Wizards of the Coast. And his words last August gave me hope —and continue to do so, given the refreshingly straightforward candor of them.
In an interview with Wargamer's Mollie Russell , Ayoub doesn't mince words: "Bluntly, we're recovering from a lot of missteps—very loud, very public missteps. And we're not going to fix it in one year. I can talk 'til the cows come home, but we've got to show more than tell, and that is going to take some time. I'm very conscious that it's going to take a lot of time to win back the trust to the extent that I would like.
"Having said that, I think we've started strongly, and a lot of these things are still happening behind the scenes." To Ayoub's credit, there've already been some solid signs of change. After bungling its weird 3D tabletop in Sigil , D&DBeyond has focused on its already-present 2D offerings and incrementally improved it considerably .
Rather than trying to muscle out third-party competition, Wizards has also been doing extensive partnered content with those same creators, which is genuinely lovely to see. It's not all roses, mind—Hasbro has been engaging in some nasty union busting behaviour . Which didn't take , as UWOTC-CWA was formed thereafter.
Still, overall, Ayoub does seem to genuinely be walking the walk, not just talking the talk: "Honestly, if I would give myself good grades on one thing in particular over the past year, I think it's been listening. We established the community council. I've personally spent a bunch of time talking to not just fans, but retailers and consumers."
Regarding the OGL itself, Ayoub states that: "D&D is about, for, and by the fans. That's the first fundamental point that we can never lose. I think, over the course of several years, we lost sight of what was important. We lost sight of who our audience was."
Ayoub admits that the OGL fiasco "was a rug pull, right? A lot of people and businesses were built up around a specific thing. Trust was given to the brand, and people rightly felt the rug was pulled from under them. In some cases, it's caused damage we are still trying to fix today. So I understand the hesitancy of 'okay, here's this new guy saying all these things'."
"My biggest takeaway as I step into this role is that trust takes a long time to build and a second to break. I'm keenly aware it's going to take me a long time to repair this, but my hope is people will give the benefit of the doubt as we continue to show that lessons have been learned. This is a new direction, a new voice, and a new spirit and energy behind D&D."
While the grotty old cynic in me is still tutting and shaking my fist at recent crossovers , I still feel more optimistic about the system's future than I have in a long time. For one, just having its current head speak so candidly is kind of jarring—let alone the actual enthusiastic collaboration with third-party sources. The future's looking brighter by the second. Or, as Ayoub puts it, talking about bringing in partners to help write core source books:
"What was rewarding for me was, when we laid out that we want to bring all these voices back, I was thrilled with the level of excitement from these partners. It was almost like this exhale of relief."
